Q: Is `[[likely]]` redundant when `[[unlikely]]` is present in an early return if-statement? trying to omit the `else [[likely]]` optional part A:

Do not change your coding style to make use of these attributes. Write code in whatever you consider to be the ideal format, then judiciously (not excessively) add one or more of these attributes where appropriate. The semantics typically take care of the rest. Read on for more details if you are concerned your code might be atypical in this respect.

Semantics

The likely attribute means that its path of execution is arbitrarily more likely than any path of execution that lacks this attribute. The unlikely attribute means that its path of execution is arbitrarily more unlikely (less likely) than any path of execution that lacks this attribute. That means each path of execution falls into one of four categories: "likely", "unlikely", "neutral" (marked neither likely nor unlikely), and "confused" (marked both likely and unlikely). Note that "confused" code is often a sign that something is incorrect, so I'll ignore this category.

The existence of three (or four) categories can be misleading when there are only two branches of execution to consider. Thanks to the word "arbitrarily", the case of a "likely" path paired with a "neutral" path is effectively the same as a "likely" path paired with an "unlikely" path. In either case, the first path is arbitrarily more likely than the second (with no consideration as to how much more likely). Having a third category matters only when there are at least three branches, such as is often the case when there is a switch.

So there is no reason to think "the specific situation about when the else can be omitted" is special. What matters are the paths of execution, not how they are presented. In all four of the question's functions, there are the same two paths of execution with the less likely path occurring when a < 1. The more likely path is

  1. int b{0};
  2. b = b + 1;
  3. return b;

The less likely path is

  1. int b{0};
  2. return b;

Semantically, all four functions are the same. If compiled with a high enough level of optimization for the likely/unlikely attributes to have an effect, they should compile to the same machine code. The same goes for any function that provides the same two paths of execution with the same relative likelihood. For example, the following function (where I've merged the return statements) is even simpler than f4 and compiles to the same machine code after enabling optimizations.

int f5(int a)
{
    int b{0};

    if (a >= 1) [[likely]]
    {
        b = b + 1;
    }
    
    return b;
}

Expectations

if you can expect the same consistent and positive compilation behavior

No, because the behavior involves an optional optimization. It is up to each compiler to decide how and if the likelihood attributes are supported. Admittedly, if a compiler's support decreases, it likely would be considered a regression (bug), but fixing an optimization regression gets lower priority than fixing a compliance regression. If you assume good faith on the part of the compiler, you can expect that regressions will be addressed eventually, but not necessarily immediately (which you would need for "consistent" compilation behavior).

Furthermore, there is no guarantee that the result is "positive". The Standard has a relevant note:

Excessive usage of either of these attributes is liable to result in performance degradation.

Programmers are notoriously bad at guessing which branches are likely. If "positive" is important to you, you should have performance tests to verify that your use of likely/unlikely improves performance. These tests should be repeated after every compiler upgrade to detect regressions. If the code is not a performance bottleneck, running these tests might be more work than is warranted, but that is up to you.

In summary, test instead of expect, and don't let premature optimizations degrade the readability of your code.

Q: What is the difference between libc++ and libc++abi library in LLVM? A:

The Application Binary Interface, or ABI for short, is intended to provide certain low level functions from which to build the C++ standard library. It is a supporting library that is a separate component from the actual standard library. Along with libcxxabi, you may also come across Pathscale's libcxxrt or GCC's libsupcxx.

On the other hand, libc++ is an implementation of the C++ standard library that can be built using either of the 3 mentioned ABIs.

Q: Get specific row col values from mysql using vb 2012 A:

You need to instantiate the dataset that you pass to the Fill method.

....
dataset = new DataSet()
dataadapter.Fill(dataset)
...

Do not forget to close the connection when finished. It is a resource very costly to keep open when you not need it

Using sqlcon = New MySqlConnection("Data Source=localhost;Database=database;User ID=root;Password=;")

    sqlcon.Open()
    sql = "select * from account"
    dataadapter = New MySqlDataAdapter(sql, sqlcon)
    dataset = new DataSet()
    dataadapter.Fill(dataset)
    TextBox2.Text = dataset.Tables(0).Rows(0).Item(0).ToString()
End Using

See the Using Statement

However if you need only one row it is better to refine the query applying a WHERE clause to limit the results returned by the database.

    sql = "select * from account WHERE AccountName = @name"
    dataadapter = New MySqlDataAdapter(sql, sqlcon)
    dataadapter.SelectCommand.Parameters.AddWWithValue("@name", inputNameBox.Text)
    dataset = new DataSet()
    dataadapter.Fill(dataset, "Account")
    if dataset.Tables("Account").Rows.Count > 0 then 
        TextBox2.Text = dataset.Tables("Account").Rows(0).Item(0).ToString()
    End If

this hopefully will return just the row needed
